title: Ferrari become latest team to unveil special livery for US GP
excerpt:
Ferrari have become the latest team to unveil a special livery for the United States Grand Prix, with the unique design adorning both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton’s SF-26s.

Developed in close collaboration with title partner HP, the livery incorporates sketches, technical drawings and blueprint-inspired graphics in a visual tribute to the designers, engineers and technicians who work so hard to put a Formula 1 car together. According to Ferrari, the Austin design “puts the development process itself at centre stage celebrating the work that takes place long before a car reached the circuit.”

The livery project involved close collaboration between Ferrari and HP specialists, with multiple rounds of testing and refinement ensuring the graphics that will adorn the cars this weekend could be accurately reproduced. HP Latex technology was used to reproduce the blueprint- inspired graphics, continuing the work Ferrari and HP have pursued on previous special liveries.

“The livery celebrates the journey from idea to reality,” said Silvia Cavallaro, Head of Color and Trim at Ferrari. “Every Ferrari starts with creativity, sketches and engineering expertise long before the car reaches the track.

“Thanks to our collaboration with HP, we were able to bring that process to life visually and tell a story that reveals the craftsmanship and innovation behind the performance.”

Scroll through the gallery above to check out Ferrari’s special livery for the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

title: Aston Martin reveal special livery for United States Grand Prix
excerpt:
Aston Martin have unveiled a special livery that will adorn their car at this weekend’s United States Grand Prix, in celebration of the team’s five-year partnership with Cognizant.

It was back in 2021 that Cognizant first paired with Aston Martin, just as the company returned to Formula 1 after taking over the former Racing Point squad. Now, in celebration of that five-year milestone, the AMR26 will run a one-off design in Austin, marking the latest chapter after Cognizant became the team’s Global AI Services Partner earlier this year.

"Cognizant has been part of our journey since Aston Martin returned to Formula 1 in 2021, and we're incredibly proud to celebrate five years of partnership together,” said Lawrence Stroll, Executive Chairman of Aston Martin.

“A great partnership is one that continues to evolve. Over the past five years, both our organisations have changed considerably, but our shared ambition and desire to keep pushing forward have remained constant.

"The special livery in Austin is our way of celebrating that journey. It's a visible thank you to Cognizant and its people for five years of partnership, while looking ahead to an exciting next chapter together."

Check out images of Aston Martin’s special livery at the top of the page, as well as the video below.

Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez sits at more than 2,200m, where thin air strips downforce and strains cooling, placing a premium on grid position and reliability. Interlagos then packs elevation change and a compact 4.3km (2.7-mile) lap into its first weekend without a Sprint since 2019.

title: How F1 drivers and strategists tackle the Circuit of The Americas
excerpt:
The US Grand Prix at the Circuit of The Americas is one of the great tent-pole events of the Formula 1 calendar. It is simply immense, drawing in vast crowds, celebrity guests and a stupendous TV audience. It’s a superb circuit that has always produced interesting races, and right from year one has been a firm favourite with the teams.

COTA is a good place to race – but that’s not the same as being an easy place to race. The track makes harsh demands on an F1 car. It’s very fast, but also very bumpy; the first sector demands a car that works well in high-speed, but elsewhere the lap wants one that excels in low-speed – and you really can’t set-up for both.

And while engineers are dealing with that conundrum, drivers need to figure out how to approach a Qualifying lap: push too hard at the start and the tyres give up before the end. The 'Goldilocks Zone’ is as ephemeral as the morning mist in Travis County.

So how will the teams, drivers and strategists approach the weekend? It’s time to take a look in The Risk Perspective, in partnership with Marsh, Formula 1's Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

The Engineering Perspective: Xavi Marcos Padros

Xavi Marcos Padros has vast experience on both sides of the Atlantic, having worked in F1 for HRT, Williams and Ferrari, around a spell as chief race engineer for Richard Childress Racing in NASCAR. He joined Cadillac in 2025, working on its WEC and IMSA programmes, before becoming chief race engineer for the Cadillac F1 Team.

“The different sectors at COTA pose some really good questions for set-up, with no obviously right or wrong answers. A lot depends on your car: you might get the best results optimizing around the high-speed corners at the start of the lap, or around the lower speed sections at the end.

“The surface is quite rough – but that doesn’t really change our set-up discussions because we’re asking the same questions about how best to maximise what we have, no matter the limitations of any particular circuit.

“We’ll discuss damper settings, general stiffnesses to cope with any bumps, try to maximise ride-height for those, and also, of course, to make sure we are legal at the end of the race with the amount of wear to the plank [the composite board attached to the bottom of the car, which is measured post-race to ensure a minimum ride height].

“Our initial set-up for FP1 is based on simulator and simulation data, and then we’ll make adjustments for FP2, based on what we saw in FP1. We’ll have some simulator sessions overnight on Friday to optimize the setup for Saturday, but we’ll also take into account the drivers’ feedback. Some can cope with a stiffer set-up, others need something a little softer. We’ll factor all of these things into our decisions.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the US Grand Prix

“Getting a Qualifying lap right is very difficult, because there are risks involved. It is a tough lap for the tyres: if the out-lap prepares them well so they are ready for the first sector then they overheat in the final sector, which is very tough on the left side of the car through the long right-hand corners.

“We can compromise, and perhaps do the first sector with tyres that aren’t quite up to temperature, so they are better in the final part of the lap – but it can be difficult to know which is the best approach. We’ll practice this on Friday, trying different sorts of out-lap, and than plan a cross-car test for our final Qualifying sims in FP3… but it can be a moving target because rubber will go down, grip will increase and the track will evolve."

The Strategy

In strategy terms, COTA has tended to be one of the more interesting circuits on the F1 calendar, being on the cusp between one and two stops. Between 2021-23 it was a two-stop race, being won by medium>hard>hard in ’21, medium>hard>medium in ’22, and medium>medium>hard in ’23.

For 2024 it dropped to a medium>hard one-stop and, last year, Pirelli tried something different with a compound bridge: instead of the usual C2-C3-C4, they bought C1-C3-C4, with the hope of a tortoise-and-hare scenario, of steady one-stoppers using the hard compound battling in the final laps with the more rapid two-stoppers running the softer compounds.

It didn’t work out that way, with the race being entirely a one-stop affair… on the softer tyres, Max Verstappen won with a medium>soft race. This year, Pirelli go back to the conventional C2-C3-C4.

The race we get at COTA often depends on the temperatures, with Texas at the end of October capable of going either way. At the time of writing, the forecast is for hot weather, which tends to increase degradation, but two-stop races have been a rarity in 2026…

The Drivers’ Perspective: Colton Herta

Colton Herta is Cadillac’s test and reserve driver, and will be taking part in FP1 this weekend, substituting for Sergio Perez for one of the team’s mandatory rookie sessions. This is his fourth FP1 session of the season, having already appeared in Barcelona, Budapest and at Monza.

Despite being only 26, he has vast experience as a racing driver, having completed seven series in IndyCar, winning nine times and finishing second in the 2024 Championship. The first of his nine victories came here at COTA, back in 2019 – when he became the youngest driver to ever win in IndyCar.

“The right set-up is always a difficult question to answer for this track because the different sections ask quite different things of the car. One of the biggest challenges is how bumpy it is and finding the right balance between ride heights and overall stiffness. You’re trying to get something that works well through the high-speed first sector but still gives you what you need in the longer, slower corners.

“Wind can also change which parts of the track you can maximize, so that adds another factor to think about. With the unusual mix of corners, you’re never going to feel completely comfortable or happy everywhere. It’s about finding a happy medium across the whole lap.

“The biggest thing you have to remind yourself is that you’re never going to feel completely comfortable on a lap here. That’s just part of the challenge of driving at COTA, and you have to keep that in mind when you’re judging how the car feels.

“From a set-up point of view, you’re trying to find the best compromise between dealing with the bumps and getting the balance you want around the rest of the lap. You can work towards something that feels as good as possible, but it never feels perfect everywhere. There’s always a bit of give and take, and you have to get comfortable with that compromise.

“For me on Friday, the track knowledge will definitely help. Having raced there before gives me a reference for the layout and the different sections – although it’s been seven years since I was last here, so I’m sure the bumps have changed in that time!

“There are similarities and differences between driving an F1 car and an IndyCar, and some of that familiarity with the circuit will carry over. At the same time, you have to be open to what each car needs from you. I haven’t been able to compare the two cars on the same track yet, so it will be interesting to see where the approach feels similar and where you need to adapt.”

The Key Section: Turn 19

COTA provides thrills and spills at Turns 1 and 12, but the corner that really does the heavy lifting is Turn 19. The penultimate corner is a quick, open left-hander, turning through 90°, with a tendency to fling cars out wide into the run-off. Slightly downhill on entry, it’s very difficult to judge.

It comes at the end of the stadium section, when the tyres are really protesting, and anyone who’s taken a little too much out of the rubber runs the risk of running off on exit and collecting a track limits penalty.

On race day, it’s produced some spectacular attack and defence. The previous three turns are cumulatively one long right-hand bend, and often cars will approach T19 side-by-side, and have to settle their differences in braking and line for the corner – much to the delight of the large grandstand sited here.

Another facet of the corner is where it sits in relation to the all-important detection points. In years past, the DRS detection point for the main straight came just in front of the braking zone for T19. This year, the Overtake Mode detection point comes after it – so following closely through this corner is going to be important – but in a slightly different way.

The Greatest Race: 2015 US Grand Prix

The US Grand Prix has had more than its fair share of gripping title deciders and close finishes, but limiting ourselves to just the races at COTA, then the 2015 US Grand Prix really stands out, thanks to a lady named Patricia.

Patricia was a Category 5 hurricane that battered the western coast of Mexico. It was a monster, with record wind speeds and the lowest sea-level pressure recorded in the Western Hemisphere. COTA didn’t get the full force, but the City of Austin received torrential rains and flooding.

FP1 and FP3 were wet, FP2 was cancelled. Qualifying was washed-out, postponed until Sunday morning and then cancelled after Q2. Going in, Lewis Hamilton led the Drivers’ Championship with Mercedes team mate Nico Rosberg and Ferrari’s Sebastian Vettel still in mathematical contention.

Rosberg took pole, Hamilton second and Vettel, courtesy of an engine penalty, starting 13th. The race featured a wet start, the only dry running of the weekend, two Safety Car periods, two Virtual Safety Car Periods and six changes of the lead.

A start on intermediate tyres saw Hamilton grab the lead, nerfing Rosberg into the run-off at Turn 1 in the process. He was down to fifth, but the craziness of the first lap saw a VSC deployed to allow marshals to sweep up debris. With the track drying, the Red Bulls of Daniel Ricciardo and Dany Kvyat had all the pace. Danny Ric passed his team mate and then both Mercedes to take the lead on Lap 15.

Hamilton was the first of the leading pack to pit for slicks, coming in on Lap 18. Ricciardo, Rosberg and Kvyat followed the next time around, all coming out ahead of Hamilton. The advantage reversed on the slicks, however, and first Rosberg and then Hamilton were able to pass the Red Bulls and take the lead of the race.

A Lap 27 Safety Car compressed the field again, then another VSC came out on Lap 38 for more debris. Rosberg came in for a second stop. Hamilton assumed the lead, making his second stop on Lap 43 under a full Safety Car after a massive shunt for Kvyat, handing the lead back to Rosberg.

The final interruption bunched the field, effectively turning the race into a ten-lap sprint. Rosberg held his lead at the restart, but a lap later and under pressure, ran wide, allowing Hamilton to finally and decisively retake the lead, win the race, take the title, and let everyone else breathe again.

The Strategic Masterstroke

2021 US Grand Prix – Verstappen’s well-informed undercut

The stakes were high in 2021, with reigning champion Lewis Hamilton and young pretender Max Verstappen locked in battle for the Drivers’ title. Max had taken the lead of the Championship at the previous round in Turkey, and the fight resumed at COTA with Max taking pole position, with Lewis right alongside.

Hamilton made the better start and took the lead through a closely contested first corner, but the race was always going to be decided on pit stops. Degradation was expected to be high, which creates conditions for both a two-stop race and also a very powerful undercut. The risk with the undercut, however, is going too early.

There’s both the simple equation of having to extend the subsequent stints, but also the need to push the tyres straight out of the wrapper to make the undercut effective, contrary to the best use of the tyre which demands a gentle introduction for a long life. Unable to find a way through, Verstappen pitted on Lap 10 – first of the leaders to pull the pin. Hamilton waited until Lap 13 and came out six seconds behind.

Both drivers were planning a medium>hard>hard race. Lewis closed the gap but Max once again jumped early, this time pre-empting an undercut by stopping on Lap 29. Hamilton, in free air, ran to Lap 37, building a big tyre delta to ensure a good pace advantage for the final stint.

He came out nine seconds behind and again started closing the gap… but not fast enough. Verstappen had enough life left in his tyres to eke-out his lead, keeping Hamilton out of DRS range until the penultimate lap. He and Red Bull had judged the life of the hard compound perfectly.

This wasn’t down to luck. One of the inherent risks of the modern tyre allocation is that each car only gets two sets of hard compound tyres, which, at high-deg tracks, often gives teams a difficult choice to make: use a set in practice and go into the race with good information but only one set of hards, or save both for the race and effectively go in blind.

Mercedes, in common with McLaren, Ferrari, Williams, and AlphaTauri, elected save their hards for the race; Red Bull decided to learn about the tyre in practice – but only on Sergio Perez’s car. The Mexican driver was not entirely thrilled with his sacrificial role – but it enabled his team to win the Grand Prix.

The Risk Perspective is brought to you in association with Marsh, Formula 1’s Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

title: Vesti on the unusual way he became a Mercedes Junior driver
excerpt:
Mercedes’ Third Driver Fred Vesti has shared an insight into the unusual way that he became a part of the squad’s Junior Programme, as well as reflecting on why he feels “deep in my heart” that there will be a seat for him on the F1 grid in the future.

Vesti was competing in his second season of Formula 3 in 2021 when he was signed up as a Mercedes Junior – a pathway that occurred after he found a way to quiz Team Principal Toto Wolff at an event away from the racetrack.

“I had followed Toto in Germany in Hockenheim,” Vesti explained on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid. “I knew he was coming to a party. I was almost like a journalist at the red carpet.

“I stopped him at the red carpet and I asked him, ‘How do I become a junior driver with you?’ That was how I started the conversation with Mercedes. I just had this vision of being a Mercedes Junior and it could take me all the way to Formula 1, so yeah, it was a very different way of approaching a junior programme.

“I think he respects that a lot and I think he respects passion massively, and if he can see that you are motivated beyond anything he has seen before, I think that's where you make the difference. It wasn't easy getting signed by Mercedes at this point.

“One of the reasons why I really liked the Mercedes Junior Programme was actually because they only had a few drivers. They had George [Russell] and a couple of other drivers and that was it. So to be a Mercedes Junior driver is something very few people get to do.”

Since getting signed to the squad, Vesti – who went on to finish as runner-up in the 2023 Formula 2 championship – became a reserve driver from 2024 onwards, which has seen him participate in FP1 sessions for the team as well as undertaking plenty of simulator work.

The role also means that Vesti works closely with Russell and Kimi Antonelli, with the Dane admitting that, when it comes to the difference in their driving styles: “For me as the third driver in the sim, I sort of have to do both.

“I have to balance both drivers because we are equally using their data. I think Kimi, one thing that he does quite a lot is he sends in a lot of speed into the corner, which, with this car, it seems to work really well. George in some ways backs it up a bit more, focusses on the exit, but it's not as simple as this because it changes weekend to weekend, corner to corner.”

And while Vesti is currently focused on supporting Mercedes’ main drivers each race weekend, the 24-year-old is still chasing his own F1 dream, a goal that he feels confident he can achieve.

“It's a very unforgiving job as third driver,” he explained. “You are helping making champions but it's not yourself. Obviously, I've had my own dreams of racing in Formula 1 since I was a kid and that dream is still very much alive. The team sees me as a Formula 1 driver.

“Sometimes they say, ‘Fred you're not a rookie, you have done so much testing, you are so prepared for a Formula 1 seat’, so I'm living and breathing like a Formula 1 driver. That's the trust I have from the engineers first of all.

“They need a lot of trust in the driver that they lean on if that [stepping in for Russell or Antonelli] would happen, and it's taken me some good time, some years to become the driver I am today and to be ready for that scenario.

“I'm working with the best engineers, the best drivers in the world and I'm really improving rapidly as a driver towards Formula 1. My dream is to be on the grid, winning races, fighting for championships in Formula 1 and that's what I wake up thinking about every morning.

“I'm working so hard for it. I have this feeling so deep in my heart that there is a seat for me, and I am so hungry and ready to do anything to achieve that goal. The goal is a Formula 1 seat and I can feel it's coming.”

title: What tyres will the teams have for the United States GP?
excerpt:
Next up on the 2026 F1 calendar is the United States Grand Prix, held at Austin's Circuit of The Americas – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

For this year's event, the C2 has been selected as the hard compound, with the C3 as the medium and C4 as the soft. This marks a change from last season, when Pirelli brought three non-consecutive compounds (the C1, C3 and C4) for what was a Sprint weekend.

The usual Grand Prix format is in place this time around, so drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The Austin circuit, which is 5.513km long, features a mix of high-speed corners, rapid direction changes and slower sections that demand strong traction," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "To be competitive, teams must combine good straight-line speed with efficient aerodynamic load through the more technical sections, an aspect that becomes even more important with the current generation of Formula 1 cars.

"From a tyre perspective, COTA places demands on both axles. In the first sector, characterised by fast corners and direction changes inspired by some of Europe’s great circuits, the front tyres will be placed under particular stress. In the third sector, meanwhile, the numerous acceleration zones out of slow corners will tend to generate thermal degradation primarily on the rear tyres.

"The asphalt surface is not particularly abrasive. A section of the circuit between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced earlier this year. However, the ageing effect on the remainder of the track continues to be significant and contributes to high wear levels. Tyre wear, rather than graining, could therefore prove to be one of the key factors over the weekend. During last year's event, several tyres reached very high wear values.

"Track grip is generally good, aided by the support categories, including the Porsche Carrera Cup North America, which has been supplied by Pirelli since the start of this year. Track evolution, on the other hand, has traditionally not been among the most pronounced on the calendar.

"From a strategic standpoint, the presence of the C2 as the hard compound could favour long stints, offering teams a solid option for what is likely to be a one-stop race. However, the high temperatures that typically characterise the Texan weekend must also be taken into account, as they could increase degradation and open the door to alternative strategies."

For more information about Pirelli’s F1 tyres, visit pirelli.com.

title: What is the weather forecast for the United States Grand Prix?
excerpt:
Formula 1 heads to Austin this weekend for the United States Grand Prix, the first stop on a triple header in the Americas – but what kind of weather conditions will the drivers and teams face?

A warm 2025 event saw Max Verstappen take a commanding victory to slash Oscar Piastri's lead in the standings, with the Australian settling for fifth place behind his McLaren team mate Lando Norris in P2, and the Ferrari pair of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The Red Bull driver is on a superb run of form this time around too, having won the most recent Grands Prix in Malaysia and Singapore, and it looks like he'll have to tackle the hot weather in Austin once again as he targets a fifth victory at the track.

Scroll down for a more detailed look at the forecast for the United States Grand Prix.

2026 United States Grand Prix weekend weather forecast

FRIDAY, OCTOBER 23 – FP1 AND FP2

Conditions: The weather on Friday is expected to be warm and dry. Daytime temperatures will range from 16°C to 29.5°C, with track temperatures peaking above 55°C. South to southeasterly winds will be moderate, averaging around 10 km/h with occasional gusts up to 30 km/h, and no rain is anticipated, ensuring ideal conditions for both practice sessions.

Maximum temperature expected: 29 Celsius

Minimum temperature expected: 16 Celsius

Chance of rain: 0%

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24 – FP3 AND QUALIFYING

Conditions: Expect warm and dry conditions with building cloud cover throughout the day. Temperatures will range from 17°C in the morning to a high of 29.5°C in the afternoon, with track temperatures likely exceeding 55°C again, given ample sunshine early. Winds will average 15 km/h, with gusts up to 35 km/h possible, and no precipitation is anticipated, ensuring dry conditions for the final practice session and Qualifying.

Maximum temperature expected: 29 Celsius

Minimum temperature expected: 17 Celsius

Chance of rain: 0%

title: Liam Lawson handed emphatic backing to keep Racing Bulls F1 seat
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has been one of the standout performers in F1 this season, but his future is still not sewn up, and Red Bull has three strong candidates for the two Racing Bulls seats.

Neither Lawson nor team-mate Arvid Lindblad, who has also impressed in what is his rookie year, has been confirmed for the 2027 campaign, and with F2 title contender Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings, the top brass at the joint Milton Keynes-Faenza team has a tough choice to make.

It is, of course, a good position to be in, but there is considerable speculation surrounding what decision might be made.

Lindblad is broadly expected to keep his drive, given his age and trajectory, with the likely call being made between Lawson and Tsolov.

Tsolov is just seven points behind Haas-bound Rafael Camara in the F2 drivers' standings, and will not be able to return to the series next term if he does win the crown.

However, he has little experience in an F1 car, and a year on the sidelines as Racing Bulls reserve driver may be the best course of action, F2 title or not.

Lawson, meanwhile, is well on his way to clinching 'best of the rest', sitting ninth in the F1 drivers' table as the highest-placed driver from outside the top four teams.

Whilst 14 of his 75 points have come for Red Bull, he has almost double the number of points of Alpine's Pierre Gasly in tenth.

As such, in a recent poll conducted by RacingNews365, over 70 per cent of respondents agreed that Lawson has done enough to earn his Racing Bulls seat for next year.

title: Lewis Hamilton cruelly denied historic F1 title in tense showdown
excerpt:
19 years ago, a rookie Lewis Hamilton was denied his first F1 title in agonising circumstances.

In one of the most dramatic F1 title showdowns in the sport's history, Lewis Hamilton was cruelly denied a maiden championship in just his rookie season.

On this day 19 years ago, the Brazilian Grand Prix marked the final round of the season.

Hamilton entered the event needing only fifth place to become F1's youngest world champion, only to watch the title slip away in the space of a few chaotic laps at Interlagos.

The McLaren rookie had led the drivers' championship into the finale, but a difficult opening lap set the tone for his afternoon.

Hamilton locked up behind Fernando Alonso as he tried to avoid contact, running wide and dropping down the order. Worse was to come on lap eight, when his MP4-22 unexpectedly selected neutral and coasted for around 30 to 40 seconds before the gearbox reset itself, dropping him as low as 18th.

McLaren later insisted the fault stemmed from an internal gearbox default rather than driver error, though the exact cause was never fully resolved.

The team switched Hamilton to an aggressive three-stop strategy in an attempt to salvage the result, but it left him short, with the Briton crossing the line seventh. That was not enough.

Kimi Raikkonen, who had trailed Hamilton by seven points heading into the race, used an overcut during Ferrari's second round of pit stops to leapfrog teammate Felipe Massa and take victory, snatching the title by a single point.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

What was said?

Hamilton reflected on a brutal finish to his debut season, stating: “It wasn't a great start to the race, I locked up behind Fernando basically to avoid hitting him and went a bit wide.

“I came back on and was quite relaxed, I knew that I had the pace."

He struck a philosophical tone when assessing the bigger picture.

"For sure we led the World Championship all the way to the last race and we had a tough three weeks, there was nothing we could do. We did the best job we could, the team did a phenomenal job all year.

“The car was great and I honestly still believe that we have the quickest car and I think we've learnt so much from this year, we'll go into next season with our heads high and I know I will do even a better job next year and come back even stronger."

Alonso, who finished third, conceded the title belonged to his rival. "The result today is of course disappointing but we already knew that it would be difficult starting from fourth to win the race and the Championship today.

McLaren subsequently appealed fuel temperature irregularities on the Williams and BMW Sauber cars, a case that could theoretically have handed Hamilton the crown.

The FIA's International Court of Appeal threw it out weeks later, with Jean Todt declaring that "a final and desperate attempt to change the result obtained on the track was rejected."

title: FIA scraps removal of F1 power unit rule change after tweaks to regulations
excerpt:
F1 introduced more leeway for power unit components for the 2026 season, the first of the new regulations cycle. This exception was due to last just one year, but has now been extended to the 2027 and 2028 rules.

Formula 1's power unit manufacturers will continue to benefit from extra leeway on various components for a second and third year, with the FIA confirming the allowance introduced for 2026 will remain in place through 2027 and 2028 as well.

F1 switched to a new engine formula this year. The V6 hybrid architecture has survived, but in heavily revised form: the complex MGU-H has been scrapped, and far more emphasis now falls on the electrical side of the power unit through the MGU-K.

That overhaul, which typically brings teething troubles of its own, prompted the FIA and Formula 1 to soften the rules slightly for 2026.

Every team was permitted one additional unit of each engine component, giving manufacturers some breathing room before grid penalties came into play.

The exception was always intended as a bridge through the early years of the new regulations. The 2026 rulebook stated explicitly that the extra unit allowance would apply for that season only.

But the newly published regulations for the 2027 season show a change of plan. Article B8.2.3 of the sporting regulations now states that all drivers may use one additional example of each power unit element listed in Article B8.2.2, for the 2026, 2027 and 2028 seasons alike.

What it means for drivers and teams in 2027 and 2028

Drivers will be able to use four internal combustion engines, four turbochargers, four exhaust systems, three energy stores, three control electronics units, three MGU-Ks and six power unit ancillary components across those campaigns. Without the extension, each of those allocations would have dropped by one unit.

The decision to carry the exception into 2027 and 2028 appears to stem from the subtle but significant tweaks still being made to the power unit rules over the coming seasons.

The internal combustion engine currently supplies 53 per cent of total power output, with the electric motor contributing 47 per cent.

That split shifts to 58/42 in 2027, before moving to a final 60/40 ratio in 2028.

The change brings higher fuel flow requirements, which is why grand prix distances will be trimmed from 305 kilometres to 290 kilometres from 2027, Monaco aside, where the race has always been run over 260 kilometres.

Race distances are set to return to their usual length from 2028, though it remains unclear exactly which technical adjustments to the cars will be needed to make that possible.

title: Aston Martin uncover celebratory livery tweak for US Grand Prix
excerpt:
Aston Martin will race with a one-off livery at the United States Grand Prix to celebrate five years of partnership with Cognizant, the team has announced.

The design marks a relationship that began in 2021, when Cognizant joined Aston Martin as the marque returned to the F1 grid.

The livery will take to the race track at the Circuit of the Americas this weekend, and will celebrate the partnership between the two outfits across the last handful of years.

Aston Martin sit bottom of the constructors' standings with just seven points after 17 rounds, well adrift of the midfield battle.

The campaign has been complicated by well-documented Honda power unit deficiencies, including early-season vibration issues that risked driver nerve injury and left the team with substantial straight-line deficits compared to its rivals.

Aston Martin is not the only team marking Austin with fresh colours. Haas has revealed a Godzilla-themed livery in collaboration with TOHO, Cadillac has unveiled a Texas-inspired design on its MAC-26, and Mercedes has shown off a MANUFAKTUR-branded look for its W17.

Ferrari is also expected to reveal a special design for the weekend.

“Cognizant has been part of our journey since Aston Martin returned to Formula One in 2021, and we're incredibly proud to celebrate five years of partnership together,” said team owner Lawrence Stroll.

“A great partnership is one that continues to evolve. Over the past five years, both our organisations have changed considerably, but our shared ambition and desire to keep pushing forward have remained constant.”

“The special livery in Austin is our way of celebrating that journey. It's a visible thank you to Cognizant and its people for five years of partnership, while looking ahead to an exciting next chapter together.”

title: McLaren confirm 'modest' changes in 'stronger' warning to F1 rivals
excerpt:
McLaren chief technical officer and chief designer Rob Marshall has confirmed the MCL40 will receive a "modest" package of upgrades for the United States Grand Prix, aimed at fixing braking issues that have blighted the car in recent rounds.

The Woking-based squad arrives at the Circuit of the Americas off the back of a difficult run of results, with Lando Norris retiring from the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and both cars failing to score inside the top five at Sepang.

Though the team had a better weekend in Singapore, with Norris and Piastri fourth and fifth, respectively, a collision between them in the sprint soured the trip to the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

McLaren sits third in the constructors' standings on 339 points, with Mercedes and Ferrari both ahead. Crucially, Red Bull is now just seven points adrift in fourth.

Marshall explained the upgrade for Austin is targeted rather than wholesale, saying: "We're bringing a modest selection of upgrades for this event, aimed at improving some braking reliability and performance issues.

"We also have some small floor changes to test."

Austin should suit the MCL40

Marshall believes the characteristics of the Texas track play to the car's strengths after a run of rounds where McLaren has lagged behind.

"The Circuit of the Americas is physically demanding for driver and car. The series of high-speed corners with tempting kerbs generate high loads, which can unsettle the driver and cause damage," he said.

"We have all seen how difficult it is to predict the relative performance of the top teams over the last five or six races. Obviously, there are many factors in play here: cars being upgraded, cars suiting and drivers liking certain circuits, among other factors.

"The last few races have not been great for us, but I think we're getting stronger again and Austin is probably a better circuit for our car."

Marshall added that Friday practice would be used to validate the team's development tools against real-world data, with the full variety of corner types at COTA offering a useful benchmark.

"Practice will be important for correlating what we've seen in our development tools with the track," he added. "We are still learning how best to extract performance from this car. We have the full range of corner types here, so getting the best balance for the whole lap will be our main focus."

With technical regulations for 2027 set to remain largely evolutionary, Marshall indicated that much of what McLaren is learning with the current car will not go to waste once the rules shift.

"As we start looking ahead to next year, there are many things the team have learned from this first season of the new era," he said.

"The regulation changes for 2027 are quite modest, so most of the parts and philosophies on this car are relevant to the direction for next year.

"Even where the hardware itself doesn't carry across, the learning and correlation do. Every time we can compare simulation, tunnel and track results, we improve the tools and understanding we're using to develop 2027."

title: Mercedes make surprise astronaut signing to F1 team
excerpt:
Reid Wiseman, the NASA astronaut who commanded the Artemis II mission earlier this year, has been announced as an official ambassador for the Mercedes F1 team.

The retired U.S. Navy Captain led humanity's first crewed mission around the Moon in more than half a century, and the appointment formalises a relationship between Wiseman and the Brackley-based squad that has developed over recent seasons.

As part of his new role, Wiseman will work with Mercedes stakeholders, partners, employees and guests, helping to highlight the innovation and high-performance culture behind the team's operation.

The team says his experience at the forefront of human exploration will offer fresh perspective on teamwork, decision-making and resilience in environments where the gap between success and failure is razor-thin.

Wiseman said he has long seen parallels between the two worlds.

"I've always been struck by how much Formula 1 and space exploration have in common. In both worlds, success is never about one individual.

“It is built by talented teams solving difficult problems, preparing relentlessly, and trusting one another when the pressure is at its highest.

"I've been fortunate to spend time with the Mercedes F1 Team in recent seasons and have seen first-hand the culture, innovation, and determination that drives its success.

“Becoming an ambassador feels like a natural next step in a relationship that has already become very meaningful to me. I'm excited to work with the team and help tell the story of the people, technology, and mindset behind what they achieve."

During the nine-day Artemis II mission, the crew travelled 252,756 miles from Earth, becoming the first humans since Apollo 17 to see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes, and also eclipsed the Apollo 13 distance record for the furthest humans have travelled from Earth, which previously stood at 248,655 miles.

On re-entry, the Orion spacecraft hit speeds of 24,664mph before splashing down within one mile of its planned target, having covered 694,841 miles in total.

title: Date set for appeal in £64 million Felipe Massa court case against Bernie Ecclestone, F1, and FIA
excerpt:
A date has been set for a UK Supreme Court appeal hearing into the ongoing Felipe Massa £64 million court case against Bernie Ecclestone, the FIA and F1 over the 2008 world championship.

In October 2025, a three-day hearing at the UK High Court, attended by RacingNews365, was held in which evidence was put forward to Mr Justice Jay as Massa sought to be able to take his case against Ecclestone, the FIA, and F1 to a full trial of the High Court over the 2008 world championship.

Massa is not seeking to overturn the result which saw Lewis Hamilton crowned champion for the first time, but rather he is seeking £64 million in damages for loss of potential earnings as a world champion after the controversial 2008 Singapore GP.

Massa's lawyers argued that Ecclestone and senior then-FIA figures, including Max Mosley and Charlie Whiting, were aware during the 2008 season that Nelson Piquet Jr deliberately crashed in Singapore to bring out a safety car, with Massa suffering from a botched pit-stop under it, resulting in him dropping out of the points.

The central piece of evidence came from a 2023 interview Ecclestone had given, in which he claimed he had early knowledge of the crash, prior to the 2009 formal investigation.

Massa would go on to lose the title to Hamilton by just one point. Lawyers for Ecclestone, the FIA, and F1 claimed that the first they knew of the crash order was when Piquet Jr was fired in 2009 and the resulting 'crashgate' investigation.

Ultimately, Mr. Justice Jay dismissed three of Massa's claims in his ruling, but refused to strike out the claim for "tort of unlawful means of conspiracy", meaning the case could proceed to a full trial of the High Court.

However, lawyers for Ecclestone, F1, and the FIA then lodged an appeal to the Supreme Court, the final court of appeal in the UK, attempting to put a block on a full trial by dismissing the conspiracy tort.

Lord Justices Reed, Hamblen, and Richards granted this appeal on June 4th this year, with the date now set for the appeal hearing as February 2nd and February 3rd, 2027.

Should the Supreme Court decide to uphold the appeal, Massa's case will be thrown out and will not proceed to a full trial of the High Court. Should the Supreme Court reject the appeal, the trial will be held.

title: FIA president disputes Middle East 'risk' as F1 decision looms
excerpt:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has voiced confidence that F1 will finish its season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Uncertainty looms over the final two rounds of the season due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Earlier in the year, F1 postponed the events in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, with the former ultimately cancelled while the latter moved to Malaysia.

Other racing categories have opted to steer clear of venturing to that region to close out their championships, however F1 is still holding out for the possibility of staging its final two rounds as originally scheduled.

Ben Sulayem has insisted he has no concerns over safety, should they opt to stage the events.

"One thing I would say; I have my children there. I'm here, but they are there. You think I would leave them there, and I am here now with you?

"Also, you have to be sensible in this and say, 'are we going to have an issue?'

"What you read in the media is actually different than we have there. We read, and we see the TV, [and say] where is it?

"We don't have that really. Otherwise, why would I stay there? Why would I leave my family?

"But does this mean that there is nothing going to happen? I can't predict this. I can only tell you today that there is nothing, and the two races are going to happen.

"I don't think the FIA staff would be more important to me than myself and my family. But if I am there, it means I feel secure about it. But we don't know."

Recent reports have suggested that the Dakar Rally could move away from Saudi Arabia in January next year.

While Ben Sulayem insisted that it is safe to venture to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, when speaking about the Dakar Rally, he asserted the FIA is putting personnel safety as its highest priority.

"We will never take our staff or drivers or any officials to a place where we feel it is risky. No way."

Article continues below.

FIA 'ready' for Imola alternative

Should F1 ultimately not opt to race in Qatar and Abu Dhabi to close out the campaign, a replacement race has been touted.

It would see F1 venture back to Imola in Italy to close out the season and would mark the first time in almost three decades that the sport had its final race in Europe.

When asked if FIA would be ready to head to Imola, Ben Sulayem replied: "Of course, FIA is always ready.

"I told the GM to have another ready team from the FIA if there was nothing going on, but maybe some of the governments say, 'you cannot travel'. So what do we do?

"I mean, if everybody is there and then the teams are there and the FOM is running it, and suddenly we say, 'Oh, we cannot have our race director, we cannot have our stewards.

"No. You have to be ready, and you have to have another team ready, just in case."

title: Kimi Raikkonen smashes longstanding F1 records on date of greatest triumph
excerpt:
Kimi Raikkonen claimed two ancient F1 records in emphatic style on this day, 21 October, in 2018, at the United States Grand Prix.

Eleven years to the day after securing his only F1 drivers' championship, Kimi Raikkonen marked 21 October with another slice of history, winning the 2018 United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas.

In doing so, he became the oldest grand prix winner since Nigel Mansell in 1994 and the record holder for the longest gap between F1 victories.

The Finn, then 39 years old, had not stood on the top step since the 2013 Australian Grand Prix, a run of 114 races without a win.

That figure eclipsed the previous mark of 98 races set by Riccardo Patrese, who went winless between the 1983 South African Grand Prix and the 1990 San Marino Grand Prix.

Raikkonen started second on the grid behind Lewis Hamilton's pole-sitting Mercedes but made the most of Ferrari's race pace in Austin, converting it into a lights-to-flag-style victory while team-mate Sebastian Vettel fought back from adversity to finish fourth, behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, who rounded out the podium.

The result denied Hamilton, who needed to outscore Vettel by eight points, the chance to clinch his fifth drivers' title that weekend.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Kimi Räikkönen

Finnish

Years in the wilderness

The five-and-a-half-year gap between Raikkonen's wins told its own story of misfortune and misalignment.

His 2013 triumph in Melbourne came for a Lotus squad whose finances deteriorated so badly by that November that the Finn was forced to sit out the final two rounds of the season.

A return to Ferrari for 2014 brought no respite: the F14 T was hamstrung by a pull-rod front suspension layout that never suited Raikkonen's preference for sharp front-end response.

From 2015 onward, as Mercedes dominated the hybrid era, Raikkonen's chances were further squeezed by team strategies that frequently prioritised Vettel's title bids.

Patrese's own seven-year drought, by comparison, had been a product of unreliable and uncompetitive machinery through stints at Alfa Romeo and a declining Brabham outfit between 1984 and 1987, before he finally ended it at Imola in 1990 after joining Williams during its switch to works Renault power.

For Raikkonen, the win in Austin would be the last of his 21 career victories, a fitting final flourish on a date that already carried the weight of his 2007 drivers' title with Ferrari at Interlagos.

title: Qatar circuit boss delivers readiness update as double header nears
excerpt:
The CEO of Qatar's Lusail International Circuit has made it clear that preparations are in full swing to host MotoGP and Formula 1 next month, despite the ongoing tense regional backdrop.

The ongoing conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran, combined with Houthi missile and drone strikes across the Arabian Peninsula, has already disrupted the 2026 motorsport calendar, contributing to the cancellation of the Saudi Arabian GP and the relocation of the Bahrain event to Malaysia earlier this month.

A ballistic missile strike hit the Saudi Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran on October 13, roughly 160 kilometres across the Persian Gulf from Lusail, while maritime strikes near the Strait of Hormuz and aerial strikes on regional transport hubs have raised fresh concerns over potential airspace closures and freight delays.

Against that backdrop, Lusail's ability to deliver a smooth, secure double header carries added significance, with F1 and the FIA maintaining that the Qatar GP will go ahead as scheduled on November 29, while keeping Italy's Imola circuit on standby should conditions deteriorate further.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has said the governing body regards Qatar and Abu Dhabi as sufficiently secure to host races and would not send paddock personnel or drivers into areas of unmanaged danger, while Qatari authorities have reaffirmed that the country is safe and that it expects to host both events as planned.

The three-week gap between the two rounds, with MotoGP taking place on November 4-6, means the venue faces a tight turnaround, but with work continuing across grandstands, hospitality areas and the wider event infrastructure despite the backdrop of ongoing instability elsewhere in the Middle East.

Lusail International Circuit CEO Abdulaziz Ali Al-Muhannadi said preparations for the events are progressing as planned.

"We are looking forward to welcoming the world back to Lusail International Circuit in November for two of the most anticipated events on the international motorsport calendar, just three weeks apart," said Al-Muhannadi.

"Our preparations are nearing completion, with our teams focused on ensuring that every aspect of the venue is ready to deliver an exceptional experience for fans, as we do every year."

title: 2026 F1 United States Grand Prix - Austin weather forecast
excerpt:
2026 F1 United States Grand Prix - Austin weather forecast

The upcoming United States Grand Prix at Austin will feature friendly conditions for F1 drivers - and provide a potential overtaking aid.

The weekend in Texas is currently forecast to be dry, with temperatures in the high-20s Celsius region, possibly tipping over to the low 30s on Saturday.

There are currently two rain cells of note appearing on weather radars, with one being to the south in the Gulf of Mexico, but is not expected to move inland from Galveston Bay up to Austin.

The other is trapped by the Rocky Mountains and will be present to the northwest of Texas throughout the weekend. Although some leading-edge cloud might drift towards the Texan state capital, the main rain cells will not.

Crucially, drivers can expect an overtaking aid in the form of a headwind into the iconic raised Turn 1 braking zone.

The straight-finish straight and approach to Turn 1 at Austin run to the south-east, which is where the wind is set to come from throughout the weekend, thus meaning a head-wind will be present, which will allow drivers to brake later into Turn 1 and try to pass rivals.

For the other major overtaking spot, at Turn 12 at the end of the back straight, which runs north-east to south-west, drivers will be greeted with a crosswind from left-to-right in the braking zone.

title: FIA introduces strict new rule to shut F1 budget cap loophole
excerpt:
The FIA has introduced a brand-new article in the operational regulations for the upcoming F1 season. This is intended to prevent teams from using workarounds to have staff work on the Formula 1 project while they are officially part of a different department.

The FIA has introduced a brand new article into the operational regulations aimed at stopping Formula 1 teams from using back-door routes to keep staff effectively working on their F1 project while officially sitting under a different division.

Formula 1 teams have operated under a budget cap since 2021, limiting how much they can spend developing a faster car and forcing them to prioritise where that money goes.

There are a handful of exceptions, including driver salaries and the pay packets of the three best-remunerated senior figures at each outfit, but beyond that, salaries are included, and teams have found it far harder to simply hire more people in the search for small performance gains.

Several teams run separate divisions that work on projects outside Formula 1 entirely, though suspicion has lingered for some time that data could still be passed across to benefit the F1 operation. Red Bull has its Advanced Technologies arm, Aston Martin runs Performance Technologies, and Mercedes has its Applied Sciences division.

To prevent information from those divisions from actually making its way back to the F1 team, the FIA has decided to introduce an entirely new article into the operational regulations from the 2027 season.

The article, titled Physical and IT Segregation Between F1 Activities and Non-F1 Activities, requires teams to strictly separate their F1 operations from non-F1 activities, both physically and digitally.

That means staff will no longer be able to simply share workspaces and IT systems, and access to technical data will need to be tightly controlled.

Restrictions will also apply to shared facilities. Certain equipment, such as simulators, wind tunnels and test rigs, can still be used by both groups, but in principle not at the same time.

Teams will additionally be required to manage and log access rights, allowing the FIA to check that the rules are being followed.

[Article continues below]

Stricter rules on data and staff

The FIA will also be given explicit powers to check compliance through on-site inspections and forensic IT audits. Teams will not be permitted to get around the rules by swapping technical information via messaging apps, external storage devices, outside service providers or intermediaries.

From 1 January 2027, they will also be required to keep records of access rights and digital audit trails, so the governing body can verify compliance retrospectively.

The separation goes beyond simply keeping workspaces apart. The exchange of digital results and technical information will also be bound by strict conditions.

In certain cases, information from F1 staff may be passed to employees working on non-F1 activities, but only under specific conditions and with the required approval and documentation. The reverse transfer is not permitted.

The FIA has also set conditions for staff moving between F1 and non-F1 activities. Depending on the direction of the move, mandatory periods will apply during which they cannot carry out certain work or access relevant systems and data.

Through these measures, the FIA wants to stop teams exploiting the boundaries between different activities to indirectly share technical knowledge or resources. Responsibility for actually enforcing the separation lies with the teams themselves.

Article F6 is intended to tighten oversight of the divide between F1 and non-F1 activities, contributing to a fairer application of the sport's financial and technical regulations.

The key question now is how much teams running these kinds of external divisions will need to change their working practices to fall in line with the new rule.

title: Honda to reach major F1 milestone at 'demanding' US Grand Prix
excerpt:
Honda will become just the fifth F1 engine manufacturer to reach the milestone of 500 grand prix entries at this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

From its first entry at the 1964 German GP, Honda engines have been entered into a further 498 races, with the half-millennium coming up in Austin, Texas, in the Japanese manufacturer's latest venture into grand prix racing, with the Aston Martin squad.

Although it is Honda's 500th race entry, it is not Honda's 500th race start, with the 'missing race', as ever, being the 2005 United States Grand Prix at Indianapolis.

Honda was one of the Michelin teams that day which peeled off into the pits at the end of the formation lap, therefore meaning Jenson Button and Takuma Sato were officially credited with 'Did Not Starts'.

Honda will join Ferrari, Renault, Mercedes, and Ford-Cosworth in reaching 500 entries, with BMW sixth on the list, despite not having competed in grand prix racing since its 2009 withdrawal.

Looking ahead to the weekend, Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara spoke of the "privilege" Honda faces.

"The United States Grand Prix in Austin is always a special event, with a fantastic atmosphere and passionate fans," he said.

"This year, we have the privilege of celebrating 500 races in Formula 1, which brings more excitement and pride to the weekend.

"The Circuit of the Americas is a demanding circuit that combines fast and flowing sections with heavy traction zones.

"After the Singapore Grand Prix, our power unit and trackside staff travelled to HRC Sakura in Japan to review the last three events and prepare for another triple-header.

"Our power units have been fully serviced and are ready for Austin, where we will give it our utmost with the package we have."
